name: Alex Berger
bio: Alex Berger is a UX designer and web developer from Graz, Austria. For more than eight years he has helped local businesses, cultural organisations and start-ups turn complex services into simple, friendly websites.
additionalBio: At CreativePixel Studio he leads small design teams and works closely with developers, so ideas move quickly from sketch to working prototype. In his free time he enjoys photography, travelling and teaching beginners how to build their first website.
abstract: Simple does not mean empty. Alex shows how to remove noise from an interface step by step: clear priorities, fewer choices and honest labels. He shares before-and-after examples from real projects and a short checklist you can use the next day.

name: Jane Smith
bio: Jane Smith is an accessibility designer at Inclusive Design Lab in Vienna. She helps public institutions and companies make their websites and apps usable for everyone, including people who use screen readers, keyboards or screen magnification.
additionalBio: Before moving into design, Jane worked as a front-end developer, so she likes practical solutions that teams can apply right away. She regularly tests products together with people with disabilities.
abstract: Accessibility is not an extra feature added at the end of a project. Jane explains the small, everyday decisions that make the biggest difference: readable text, good colour contrast, keyboard navigation and clear form labels. Live demos with a screen reader show how users actually experience our designs.

name: John Miller
bio: John Miller is a UX researcher at Fieldnote Research in Munich. He plans and runs interviews, usability tests and field studies for digital products in health, mobility and education.
additionalBio: John believes that good research does not need a big budget. He enjoys showing teams how to talk to users early, test rough ideas and turn what they learn into better design decisions.
abstract: What people say they want and what they actually need are often two different things. John introduces simple research methods such as short interviews, observation and quick prototype tests. You will learn how to ask better questions and how to share findings so the whole team can use them.
